Keywords: deployment gate, approval gate, quality gate, release gate
Guidance: Deploying to production purely on 'CI passed' with no additional gate (smoke test, canary check, manual approval for high-risk changes) misses failure modes that only show up under real traffic.
Do: Layer deployment gates appropriately to risk: automated smoke tests always, manual approval for high-blast-radius changes.
Don't: Treat 'unit tests passed' as sufficient signal to auto-deploy any change straight to production.

Keywords: artifact promotion, build once deploy many, immutable artifact
Guidance: Rebuilding from source separately for each environment (dev, staging, prod) means the artifact actually tested in staging isn't guaranteed to be bit-identical to what deploys to production.
Do: Build a single immutable artifact once, then promote that exact artifact through each environment without rebuilding.
Don't: Rebuild from source code for each environment's deployment, risking drift between what was tested and what ships.
Example: docker tag myapp:1234 myapp:staging && docker tag myapp:1234 myapp:prod # same image, different labels

Keywords: rollback, rollback plan, deployment failure recovery
Guidance: Discovering how to roll back a bad deployment for the first time during an actual incident wastes critical minutes; the rollback path needs to be tested and fast before it's needed.
Do: Define and regularly test an explicit rollback mechanism (previous artifact redeploy, feature flag kill switch) before it's needed in an incident.
Don't: Design a deployment pipeline with no tested rollback path, discovering the process for the first time during an outage.

Keywords: canary deployment, blue-green deployment, progressive rollout
Guidance: Deploying a new version to 100% of traffic simultaneously means any bug affects every user at once, with no way to catch it on a small subset first.
Do: Use canary (small percentage first) or blue-green (parallel environment cutover) deployment for user-facing services where a bad release is costly.
Don't: Deploy every change directly to 100% of production traffic with no progressive rollout mechanism.
Example: # canary: route 5% traffic to new version, monitor error rate, then ramp to 100%

Keywords: pipeline secrets, secret injection, ci secrets exposure
Guidance: Echoing secrets to build logs, or storing them as plaintext pipeline variables visible to all pipeline maintainers, is a routine source of credential leaks in CI/CD systems.
Do: Use the CI platform's native secret store with masking, and scope secret access to only the specific jobs/environments that need it.
Don't: Store credentials as plaintext pipeline variables visible in logs or to all repository contributors.

Keywords: pipeline as code, ci config in repo, infrastructure as code for ci
Guidance: Configuring build/deploy steps through a CI tool's web UI leaves the pipeline definition untracked and unreviewable through the normal PR process.
Do: Define pipelines as versioned code (Jenkinsfile, .github/workflows, .gitlab-ci.yml) reviewed through the same PR process as application code.
Don't: Configure critical build/deploy steps exclusively through a CI platform's web UI with no version-controlled definition.

Keywords: feature flags, trunk-based development, long-lived branch, merge conflict
Guidance: Long-lived feature branches accumulate merge conflicts and delay integration feedback; feature flags let incomplete work merge to main continuously while staying dark until ready.
Do: Prefer trunk-based development with feature flags gating incomplete functionality over long-lived feature branches.
Don't: Maintain feature branches open for weeks/months, deferring integration and multiplying merge conflict risk.

Keywords: reproducible build, build determinism, non-deterministic build
Guidance: A build that produces different output from identical source (due to unpinned dependencies, timestamps, or non-deterministic ordering) makes debugging production incidents against 'what actually shipped' unreliable.
Do: Pin all dependency versions and eliminate non-deterministic inputs (timestamps, random ordering) from the build process.
Don't: Allow floating dependency versions or non-deterministic build steps that can produce different artifacts from the same source commit.

Keywords: flaky test, ci runtime, test parallelization, slow pipeline
Guidance: A CI pipeline that takes 45+ minutes (or has flaky, non-deterministic tests) trains developers to ignore or work around it, defeating its purpose as a quality gate.
Do: Parallelize test execution, quarantine/fix flaky tests promptly, and keep the critical-path pipeline fast enough that developers actually wait for it.
Don't: Let flaky tests linger unfixed for months, training the team to re-run CI until it passes instead of investigating failures.

Keywords: deployment marker, change correlation, deployment event
Guidance: Without recording deployment events against a timeline, correlating a metric regression or incident with 'what changed' requires manually cross-referencing commit history and guessing timing.
Do: Emit a deployment marker/event (to your monitoring/APM tool) on every deploy so incidents can be correlated against exact deploy timing.
Don't: Deploy changes with no recorded event correlating deploy time to monitoring dashboards, forcing manual correlation during incidents.

Keywords: sbom, artifact signing, supply chain security, provenance
Guidance: Deploying artifacts with no signature or provenance record means there's no way to verify a production artifact actually came from your CI pipeline and wasn't tampered with in transit or storage.
Do: Sign build artifacts (e.g. with Sigstore/cosign) and generate an SBOM, verifying signatures before deployment.
Don't: Deploy container images or binaries with no signature verification or provenance tracking.

Keywords: schema migration, backward compatible migration, zero-downtime deploy
Guidance: Running a breaking schema migration in lockstep with application code deployment causes an outage window where old app code runs against new schema (or vice versa) during a rolling deploy.
Do: Design migrations to be backward-compatible (expand/contract pattern) so old and new application versions can both run against the schema during a rolling deploy.
Don't: Ship a breaking schema change (column rename/drop) in the same deploy as the application code that depends on it.
Example: # expand: add new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, deploy code that reads only new, contract: drop old column
